titre: Ada Lovelace's Note G: A Published Program, but Not the First One Written
accroche: In 1843, Ada Lovelace publishes a program for Babbage's machine. He had written some as early as 1837, but had published none.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1843, the British journal *Taylor's Scientific Memoirs* publishes a table of numbers, letters, and operations that is now regarded as the earliest computer program. It is signed with the initials A.A.L., those of Ada Augusta Lovelace. It describes, step by step, how Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine would calculate Bernoulli numbers. The label “first programmer” has stuck to her name. It holds up less well than people think.

## What the 1843 text contains

The starting point is a memoir by the Italian military engineer Luigi Menabrea, published in French in Geneva in October 1842, reporting on a presentation by Babbage. Lovelace translates it into English and adds seven notes to it, from A to G. Together, they are about three times as long as the memoir. The last, Note G, announces that it closes the set with an example of some complexity: the calculation of Bernoulli numbers. In it she describes the state of the machine's columns for the case n = 4, with six starting data, and indicates, according to the note, that 25 operation cards suffice to obtain each Bernoulli number from the first.

## What existed before

Babbage, for his part, had written programs much earlier. Computer scientist Raúl Rojas describes in 2023 a table from 1837, in Babbage's own hand, that solves a system of two equations in two unknowns: a sequence of operations with the memory addresses of their arguments and their result, presented as the trace of a program. Historian Allan Bromley, for his part, counts several dozen examples prepared between 1837 and 1840. None was published at the time.

What distinguishes Note G, then, is not priority but publication. It is the program for the machine that the public was able to read, and an example long enough to show what the machine would be used for.

## An error, and a limit

The Note G program contains an error. At the fourth operation, the division is written the wrong way round: v5 divided by v4, instead of v4 divided by v5. Two programmers who have rewritten it in modern times, one in C, the other in Python, noticed it. It may be a simple printing typo rather than a design flaw.

In that same note, Lovelace writes that the machine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything: she herself sets the limit of the machine whose program she describes.

It remains to decide what “first” demands of a program: having conceived it, having written it, or having made it available to read.

carte.punch: In 1843, Ada Lovelace published a program for Babbage's machine, and he had already written some.
carte.idee: Babbage had written programs for his Analytical Engine as early as 1837; none had been published. Lovelace's Note G (1843), a calculation of Bernoulli numbers, is the one the public was able to read.

quiz.question: Why can't Note G be called the first program written for Babbage's machine?
choix: It reproduced word for word a program written by Menabrea
Babbage had already written programs as early as 1837, which remained unpublished
It described the Difference Engine rather than the Analytical Engine
It was never printed and circulated only in handwritten copies
quiz.explication: Babbage had prepared programs as early as 1837, including one for a system of two equations in two unknowns, without publishing them. Note G, for its part, appeared in 1843 in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs. It is not Menabrea's: his memoir is the text that was translated, not the source of the program; it concerns the Analytical Engine, like the whole set of notes; and it was indeed printed.
